findings.description: sweep moves the contract's balance of an arbitrary donated token to owner by calling transfer through the IToken interface, which declares a bool return value, and the call site never inspects that return value. Because the interface commits to a strict bool return, Solidity ABI-decodes whatever the call returns against that type. For a token that returns no data at all on transfer (the best-known real-world example is USDT on Ethereum mainnet, and this is exactly the kind of non-standard behavior the function's own NatSpec comment says it must tolerate), there is nothing to decode and the call - and the whole sweep transaction - reverts, so donations in that token can never be swept out through this function. For a token that instead signals failure by returning false without reverting, the discarded return value means sweep finishes normally even though no tokens moved, giving no on-chain signal that anything went wrong. In both cases the practical effect is the same: donated tokens of the affected type stay stuck in the contract, because sweep is the only way to move tokens out and there is no fallback rescue mechanism.

findings.recommendation: Replace the direct interface call with a defensive transfer pattern that tolerates both a missing return value and a false return value - for example OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20.safeTransfer, or an equivalent manual low-level call that requires the call itself to succeed and, only when return data is actually present, requires it to decode to true. This satisfies the documented goal of working with every ERC20-shaped token, standard or not, and turns a real transfer failure into an explicit revert instead of a silent no-op.
